findings.because: Escanciado is the Asturian ritual of pouring bottled sidra from overhead. The Basque txotx ritual is different: the cider is caught in the glass from a thin stream shot out of a freshly tapped barrel at the sagardotegi. So the accept list credits the Asturian practice as the Basque answer. The model answer's 'long high pour' has the same conflation.
findings.fix: Model answer: Caught in the glass from a thin stream shot from a freshly tapped barrel (txotx) to aerate its still, sharp body. Accept: ['caught from the barrel stream txotx', 'txotx from the barrel']
findings.verifyReason:
The examiner is right that an accept entry is wrong. The question is a-wspnxw1o in batch-005 (data-advanced.js:ADV_QUESTIONS), with the stem "Basque sidra is served by:". Its accept list includes "escanciado high pour". Escanciado, with the bottle held overhead and the glass at the waist, is the Asturian technique (eatingasturias.com: "pour cider into the glass in the Asturian manner"). The Basque cider body's own serving guide (sagardoa.eus) points the other way. It says bottled Basque cider is ideally poured "from a height of 5 to 10 cm". The signature Basque service is the txotx, where cider goes straight from the kupela (barrel) into the glass for its txinparta (sparkle). Wikipedia describes the txotx stream being caught in a glass 3 to 6 feet from the barrel.

matchSA in C:/Users/zpull/SommeliersCodex/js/core.js makes this worse. Its whole-word core rule means the input "high pour" alone matches the escanciado entry, so the grader credits the Asturian overhead pour as the Basque answer.

The model answer is only partly off. The txotx stream really is a long jet caught at a distance, but "high pour" is inaccurate. Wikipedia's loose line that Basque bottled cider is "poured from height" is not enough to save it against the Basque body's 5 to 10 cm guidance.

The examiner's fix needs two changes. First, their accept phrases are long (four words once normalised), so a candidate who types just "txotx", the most likely correct answer, would fail under the 60 percent word-coverage rule. A strict canonical entry "~txotx" fixes that. Second, the examiner's answer text calls the cider sharp, but a fix does not need to restate the taste.
findings.finalFix: Model answer (ans): "Txotx: a thin stream shot from a freshly opened barrel (kupela) and caught in the glass from a distance, to aerate the still cider". Accept: ["~txotx", "from the barrel", "straight from the barrel", "stream from the barrel", "from the kupela"]. Remove both "escanciado high pour" and "long pour from height txotx".

question.ans: The long high pour (txotx culture) to aerate its still, sharp body

findings.claim: Seven total; Duval-Leroy and Laherte bottle curiosity cuvées from the rare four.
findings.because: The Champagne cahier des charges has changed twice. From December 2022 (INAO approval, published in the JORF on 10 Dec 2022) the resistant hybrid Voltis is allowed as a 'variété d'intérêt à fins d'adaptation', capped at 5% of vineyard area and 10% of a blend. The arrêté of 31 July 2025 then added Chardonnay Rosé as a main variety, which the Comité Champagne calls the eighth recognised grape. 'Seven total' has therefore been wrong since 2022 at the latest. The stem's 'the four permitted ... beyond the big three' still holds only if it is read as the four traditional minor grapes.
findings.fix: stem: 'Name the four traditional minor Champagne grapes beyond the big three (any two).' exp: 'The historic seven; since 2022 the hybrid Voltis is allowed as an adaptation variety (max 5% of plantings, 10% of a blend), and since July 2025 Chardonnay Rosé is a main variety, so the rulebook now lists more than seven. Duval-Leroy and Laherte bottle curiosity cuvées from the rare four.'
findings.verifyReason: I opened the current Champagne cahier des charges, homologated by the arrêté of 31 July 2025 and published in the JORF on 5 August 2025. Chapter I, V.1 lists eight principal varieties: Arbane, Chardonnay, Chardonnay rose, Meunier, Petit Meslier, Pinot blanc, Pinot gris and Pinot noir. It also lists Voltis B as a 'variété d'intérêt à fin d'adaptation', held to 5% or less of the plantings on each holding and 10% or less of a blend. Voltis first entered the text through the arrêté of 30 November 2022 (JORF, 10 December 2022). The Comité Champagne press release of 16 October 2025 says Chardonnay rose has been a principal variety since 31 July 2025, 'portant à huit le nombre de cépages champenois' (bringing the number of Champagne grapes to eight). So the explanation's 'Seven total' is out of date: it has been wrong since December 2022 once Voltis is counted, and wrong on principal varieties alone since July 2025. The stem's 'the four permitted ... beyond the big three' is also no longer literally true, because Chardonnay rose is now a fifth minor principal variety and Voltis is allowed as well. The examiner's fix keeps the question on the four traditional minor grapes and states the dates and caps correctly, so the existing accept list still grades it properly.
findings.finalFix: stem: 'Name the four traditional minor Champagne grapes beyond the big three (any two).' exp: 'The historic seven; since 2022 the hybrid Voltis is allowed as an adaptation variety (max 5% of plantings, 10% of a blend), and since July 2025 Chardonnay Rosé is a main variety, so the rulebook now lists more than seven. Duval-Leroy and Laherte bottle curiosity cuvées from the rare four.'

findings.claim: further work tied that to Tribidrag, documented in Croatian records from the early sixteenth century
findings.because: Tribidrag is documented in the fifteenth century, not the sixteenth. The name appears in 1444 in a record by don Juraj Radičević, priest at Vodice in Dalmatia. The same grape appears earlier still, as Cratosia (Kratošija), in the Statute of Budva of 1426–1442.
findings.fix: further work tied that to Tribidrag, documented in Dalmatian records from the fifteenth century (1444)
findings.verifyReason: The error is real. The explanation says Tribidrag is documented from the early sixteenth century, but the name goes back to the fifteenth. ZAP's history page (Zinfandel Advocates & Producers, drawing on the Croatian research) cites a 1488 record of a barrel of Tribidrag shipped from Split to Puglia. Its 1518, 1529 and 1546 records are later references, not the first. Wikipedia gives an even earlier record: 1444, from don Juraj Radičević of Vodice. It also cites the Budva Statute (1426–1442) under the name Cratosia. The question, the model answer and the accept list are all correct; only the explanation is wrong. The examiner's fix is right about the century but pins the date to 1444. That year comes from one secondary source, while ZAP and the Croatian research literature cite 1488 as the earliest. The safer fix names the century and drops the disputed year.
findings.finalFix: further work tied that to Tribidrag, documented in Dalmatian records from the fifteenth century

question.q: Zinfandel's DNA trail ends at which Croatian variety, and what is that grape's historical name?
accept: crljenak kastelanski also known as tribidrag
tribidrag or crljenak kastelanski from croatia
crljenak kastelanski the same grape as primitivo

a croatian grape called crljenak kastelanski whose old name is tribidrag
question.ans: Crljenak Kaštelanski, later shown to be the ancient Dalmatian variety Tribidrag (Kratošija in Montenegro) — the same grape as Italy's Primitivo
question.exp: Carole Meredith's UC Davis lab matched Zinfandel to Primitivo in 1994, then in December 2001 found a handful of surviving vines called Crljenak Kaštelanski in a garden at Kaštela on the Dalmatian coast; further work tied that to Tribidrag, documented in Croatian records from the early sixteenth century. The takeaway for a candidate is that Zinfandel is an old Adriatic variety with an American career, not an American variety — which is why Primitivo tastes like a cousin rather than a copy.

findings.because: No official or standard grouping counts eleven valley-floor AVAs in Napa. Napa Valley has 17 nested AVAs (Crystal Springs of Napa Valley became the 17th in November 2024), and most of them are mountain or hillside AVAs. Only a handful straddle the floor between Highway 29 and the Silverado Trail: Oak Knoll, Yountville, Oakville, Rutherford, St. Helena and Calistoga, with Stags Leap lying east of the Trail. A candidate would learn a false count from this stem. The keyed answer itself is right.
findings.fix: The valley-floor AVAs of Napa (Oakville, Rutherford, St. Helena and their neighbours) are bisected by which two roads used in tasting shorthand?
findings.verifyReason: The stem, "The 'Eleven' AVAs of Napa's floor", puts a count in quotes as if it were a known grouping, and no such grouping exists. Napa Vintners lists 17 nested AVAs, with Crystal Springs of Napa Valley added in 2024. Most of them are mountain or upland AVAs (Atlas Peak, Chiles Valley, Diamond Mountain, Howell Mountain, Mount Veeder, Spring Mountain, Wild Horse Valley, Crystal Springs). Even a generous count of the floor AVAs gives at most nine: Carneros, Coombsville, Oak Knoll, Yountville, Stags Leap, Oakville, Rutherford, St. Helena and Calistoga. A search for "eleven" floor AVAs found no source using the figure. The stem therefore teaches a false number, and it also calls the Silverado Trail a highway. The model answer (Highway 29 on the west, Silverado Trail on the east) and the accept list are correct. The examiner has one small point wrong: the Silverado Trail runs through the Stags Leap District rather than west of it. That does not change the ruling. The proposed fix removes the false count and says "roads", which is correct.
findings.finalFix: The valley-floor AVAs of Napa (Oakville, Rutherford, St. Helena and their neighbours) are bisected by which two roads used in tasting shorthand?

question.q: The 'Eleven' AVAs of Napa's floor are bisected by which two highways used in tasting shorthand?
